ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness & UT Weld Inspection | Richmond, VA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Richmond, VA plants, boilers, tanks, bridges and fabricators. Technicians travel to site. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Richmond, Virginia
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for owners in Richmond and central Virginia: boilers and pressure vessels, steam and process piping, storage tanks, fabricated steel and bridge or crane structures. Technicians travel to your site for a defined scope and report readings against the minimum thickness or weld criteria you specify. Send drawings, materials and access notes through the UT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Richmond

Richmond sits where the James River drops over the fall line, and the region has always made things: paper and paperboard, packaging, specialty chemicals, fabricated metal products, tobacco and beverages. The city's own economic-development office counts several hundred advanced manufacturing firms and more than fifty fabricated-metal companies in the metro area. Those plants run boilers, steam headers, compressed air receivers, tanks and process piping, all of which lose wall to corrosion and erosion over years of service.

Ultrasonic thickness readings give owners a way to track that loss without shutting equipment down. The Richmond Marine Terminal on the James River adds cargo-handling steel, warehouses and storage structures, while hospitals and the university medical campus rely on steam plants and pressure systems. Add Virginia Department of Transportation steel on the interstates and river crossings, and UT reaches almost every kind of structure in the region.

Plants, terminals and bridges: the steel UT looks at

In a paper or packaging plant, the long-term targets are boiler tubes and drums, steam condensate lines, digester and dryer shells, and the chemical and liquor piping that moves aggressive fluids. In chemical and food facilities the targets are reactors, jacketed vessels, heat exchangers and storage tanks. At the terminal and at distribution centers they are crane girders, tank shells and dock structures. Fabricators in the Richmond area use UT on thick plate for lamination before forming and on groove welds once a vessel or frame is finished.

Bridge and highway steel is a different world: girders, bearings and connection plates examined under owner-specific criteria. Atlantis can collect thickness data and weld examination results on accessible structural steel, while the bridge owner or its engineer interprets condition and decides on repair.

What UT finds in central Virginia steel, and what it misses

A transducer sends a short pulse of sound into the metal, and the instrument times the echo from the far surface. Since the sound speed in steel is known, that time becomes a thickness reading. UT detects general thinning, laminations in plate, wall loss under a corroded area and, with an angled probe, flaws inside a weld. It needs access to one side only, so a vessel or line can stay online while its walls are surveyed.

The method has limits that shape any scope. Dirt, scale, thick coatings and flaking paint block the sound, so surfaces have to be cleaned to what the procedure allows. Very small isolated pits may sit between measurement points, which is why a grid is scanned rather than a single spot read. Cast iron and coarse-grained castings scatter the beam. Austenitic stainless welds are difficult for shear-wave UT because the grain structure bends and splits the sound. Tight surface cracks are better handled by magnetic particle inspection in Richmond or liquid penetrant testing in Richmond.

Codes, Virginia rules and who decides acceptance

Technique for thickness work follows ASME Section V and its SE-797 practice in Article 23, along with ASTM E797. Weld examination follows Article 4, with acceptance criteria from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessels, ASME B31.1 for power piping, ASME B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridges. ASTM E164 covers contact UT of weldments, and ASTM E114 covers straight-beam work.

Virginia puts boilers and pressure vessels under the Department of Labor and Industry, with the operating rules in Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Under the state's program, equipment must be built to ASME rules and registered with the National Board and the Department; the Department does not perform routine inspections itself, leaving that to insurance company inspectors, contract fee inspectors and owner-user inspectors who hold Virginia commissions. High-pressure boilers are inspected annually and pressure vessels every two years. Our UT readings can support those inspectors, but the statutory inspection stays with the commissioned inspector.

Where API 510, 570 or 653 applies, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible, and Atlantis supplies the examination data. Process safety rules under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 also expect mechanical integrity inspections of covered equipment, and UT is a common way to document them.

How a thickness survey is carried out in the field

We start by agreeing the locations: a grid on a shell or elbow, or fixed condition monitoring locations that will be re-read at each interval. The technician cleans the point, couples the probe with gel or paste and reads against a calibration made on a step block cut from the same material. Dual-element probes are chosen for corroded surfaces because the separate transmit and receive crystals ignore much of the roughness that confuses a single-element probe.

For a hot steam line, high-temperature probes and couplant are used and a correction is applied for the temperature of the wall, because sound slows as steel heats. The technician reads the A-scan on thin or pitted wall, where a bare digital figure can mislead through doubling or a weak echo. Each reading goes into a labeled sketch or grid, so a repeat survey measures the same spot and shows a trend rather than isolated numbers.

Angle-beam examination of welds

For weld volume, a wedge directs a shear wave into the part at an angle, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, and the technician scans the weld from each side where access allows. Indications are sized by position and amplitude, and the echo pattern as the probe moves helps separate lack of fusion, slag and cracking from geometric reflectors such as the weld root.

The construction code decides when UT is permitted as a volumetric method and what criteria apply. Where a customer wants UT to take the place of another volumetric method, we recommend agreeing that with the owner and the engineer before the job. Joint geometry, nozzle welds and thin walls often need a procedure demonstration first.

Who performs the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified under a written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician calibrates the instrument, scans, interprets and records. Procedures are approved by an ASNT Level III, and certification records are kept by the employer, which is how SNT-TC-1A works. Our founder is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and he oversees the procedure program.

Before mobilizing to a Richmond site we review drawings, materials and the code basis, and we ask about escorts, safety orientation and permit requirements at the plant. If your procedure already exists, we work to it after review, and our written practice service is available when it does not.

What the UT report contains

A UT report names the component and its identification, the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe, the calibration blocks and couplant, the surface condition and temperature, the technician and level and the date. Thickness reports include the location sketch or grid, each reading, the nominal wall and the minimum required value if provided, with readings below it flagged. Weld reports list each indication with its location, length and amplitude against the reference and the accept or reject call under the named criteria.

The report records measurements; corrosion rate, remaining life and fitness for service are decisions that belong to the owner's engineer or authorized inspector.

Planning a UT job in Richmond

Central Virginia has real seasons. Summers are hot and humid, which warms exposed steel and softens some coatings, and winter mornings can sit near freezing, which thickens couplant and chills probes. We confirm the temperature range of the procedure and bring couplant suited to the conditions. Heavy rain and thunderstorms are common in warm months, so exposed tank roofs and structures are scheduled with weather in mind.

Access usually decides the schedule. Plants require badging and orientation, confined spaces need permits, and elevated work needs scaffolding, lifts or rope access that the owner provides. Interstate access via I-95 and I-64 makes travel to most Richmond sites straightforward, while outage windows at industrial plants fill early. Tell us whether the equipment will be online, what insulation must be removed and who will do it, and a mobilized crew can be planned around those answers.

A few details sharpen the quote. List the components and their approximate locations, the diameters, wall thicknesses and materials, and whether insulation, coating or lining must be removed. Mention whether any equipment operates hot, whether the interior can be accessed and which code edition and acceptance criteria the owner has named. If your authorized inspector or engineer has specified the measurement grid or condition monitoring locations, send that plan. With those details a mobilized crew can arrive with the right probes, couplant, calibration blocks and time allowance, which keeps the survey on schedule.

Preparation before arrival makes the greatest difference to cost and duration. Insulation removal, scaffolding and surface cleaning typically take longer than the readings themselves, and arranging them ahead of the crew keeps technicians productive instead of waiting. Where several areas can be examined in one visit, bundling them reduces travel and gives you a single report set.

UT, MT or PT for your Richmond job

Pick UT when thickness, lamination or the inside of a weld is the question. Pick MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and pick PT for surface cracks in stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. A frequent combination is UT first to size a wasted area, then PT or MT on the repair weld. See the national UT service page and the ultrasonic testing guide for more background.

Training your own UT technicians

Richmond companies that want in-house UT capability can begin with UT Level 1 training and continue to UT Level 2 training. Your company issues the certification under its own written practice, and Atlantis supplies the instruction. The UT practical simulator gives trainees repetition before they scan real parts, and the Richmond training page sets out how that fits with hands-on work at your facility.

faq.q: What does UT inspection cost in Richmond?
faq.a: It depends on the scope rather than a flat figure: how many components, how easy they are to reach, how much cleaning is needed and what report you want. Send the details and we respond with a scope-based quotation.

faq.q: Can Atlantis measure boiler tube or vessel wall thickness in Richmond?
faq.a: Yes. We take thickness readings on accessible boiler, vessel and piping surfaces, record them against a grid or location sketch and flag any value below the minimum you provide. The commissioned inspector still performs the statutory inspection.

faq.q: Is UT acceptable for weld inspection under ASME and AWS codes?
faq.a: It depends on the code and the item. Some codes accept UT in place of other volumetric methods only under stated conditions, so the substitution should be agreed with the owner and engineer before work begins.

faq.q: How deep into rust or scale can ultrasound measure?
faq.a: Sound does not pass through loose scale or flaking coating. The surface is cleaned to the condition the procedure requires, and thin tight coatings may be measured through when the technique is verified on a sample.

faq.q: Can UT be performed while the equipment is running?
faq.a: Often yes, since only one side needs access. Safety rules, surface temperature and insulation removal decide whether it is practical, and hot surfaces call for high-temperature probes and a temperature correction.

faq.q: Who approves the UT procedure?
faq.a: An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and report format. The technician performing the work is a Level II qualified under the company's written practice, and the customer can supply its own procedure for review.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Richmond office?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians travel to your plant, terminal or yard, and access, orientation and permit needs are agreed with you before they are mobilized.

faq.q: What does a UT report include?
faq.a: It includes the component identification, procedure and revision, equipment and calibration, technician and level, a thickness grid or indication list and an accept or reject call against the criteria you name.

faq.q: Does UT replace a state boiler inspection in Virginia?
faq.a: No. The Virginia Department of Labor and Industry requires inspection by commissioned insurance, contract fee or owner-user inspectors. UT data can support their work but cannot substitute for the statutory inspection.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Richmond, VA | MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MT) of welds, structural steel, lifting gear and equipment at Richmond, VA plants and fabricators. Mobilized to site. Quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Richmond, Virginia
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MT, also known as mag particle testing or MPI) for Richmond and central Virginia owners and fabricators. Typical scopes include welds on carbon and low-alloy steel, structural connections, lifting gear, shafts and pins, and repair welds on pressure equipment. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send the component list and acceptance basis through the MT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Richmond

Richmond's industrial mix leans toward fabrication and process manufacturing. The metro area has dozens of fabricated-metal firms working in structural steel, plate and rebar, alongside paper and packaging mills, chemical producers and food and beverage plants. Each of those businesses welds and maintains steel structures, and each has components where a surface crack matters: hoist frames, crane runways, mixer and agitator shafts, press and conveyor parts, tank attachments and the lugs and brackets that carry equipment loads.

Transportation steel is another large field. Interstate corridors, river crossings and rail lines pass through the region, and heavy trucks, trailers and rail equipment need periodic checks of welded frames and couplings. At the Richmond Marine Terminal, handling equipment and rigging operate near the James River, and the steel is exposed to weather and fatigue. MT fits all of these because it is quick, portable and sensitive to fine cracks in ferromagnetic material.

What MT finds and what it misses

The technician induces a magnetic field in the part. Where a surface-breaking crack or a near-surface discontinuity interrupts that field, flux leaks out and fine ferromagnetic particles collect along the flaw, outlining its length and shape. MT is well suited to fatigue cracks at weld toes, quench or grinding cracks, laps and seams in forgings, and cracks that start at keyways, threads and fillets.

It can only be applied to ferromagnetic steel, including carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic or ferritic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and nickel alloys are outside its reach, and those parts go to PT in Richmond. Coatings thicker than a thin paint film reduce sensitivity, deep subsurface flaws are not shown, and a crack running along the field direction is nearly invisible, so the field must be applied in two orientations at each area.

Codes, Virginia requirements and acceptance

MT technique follows ASME Section V Article 7, summarized in our Article 7 guide, along with ASTM E709 as a guide and ASTM E1444 as a practice. Acceptance depends on the job: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.1 for power piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, AWS D1.5 for bridge steel and the owner's own specification where one exists.

The Virginia Department of Labor and Industry administers the state's boiler and pressure vessel safety program. Equipment must be built to ASME rules and registered with the National Board and the state, and operating rules are set out in Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Inspection is performed by commissioned insurance company inspectors, contract fee inspectors and owner-user inspectors. Repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code, and an MT report on a repair weld can form part of the record those inspectors review.

How the work is carried out

Weld areas are cleaned of slag, spatter, scale and oil, and loose paint is removed. For most field jobs, the technician places an electromagnetic yoke across the weld and adjacent base metal, applies the particles and watches for indications as the field is energized, then repeats at roughly right angles. Before use, a yoke is proven by a lifting check: ten pounds for an alternating-current yoke at the pole spacing in use, forty pounds for a direct-current or permanent-magnet type, and field direction is verified with an indicator.

Dry powder works well on rough, warm surfaces and on welds in the field. Wet particles, whether in visible color or fluorescent, give higher sensitivity on clean machined surfaces. Fluorescent particles need subdued light and a UV-A source with a measured intensity. If the part will be welded, machined or placed in service next to sensitive equipment, it is demagnetized afterward and the residual field is checked.

Examining structural steel and bridge-type connections

Structural steel is often examined at connection welds, flange-to-web welds, lifting attachments and repaired areas. AWS D1.1 sets acceptance criteria for building and general structural welds, while AWS D1.5 covers steel bridges and is the specification most state transportation departments apply. MT is a common surface method under both, used to look at weld toes and end terminations where fatigue cracks tend to start.

Work at height raises access issues that decide whether a job is practical. A yoke needs a stable platform and an electrical supply or battery, and a technician working from a lift or scaffold must still see the indication clearly. The structure's owner provides access and lockout; we plan the equipment, visible or fluorescent particles and lighting to suit what the platform allows.

Shafts, pins and rotating equipment

Richmond's mills and plants run a great deal of rotating machinery, and rotating parts fail by fatigue. Agitator and mixer shafts, roll journals, press columns, crusher and conveyor pulleys, pump shafts and coupling hubs are classic MT subjects because cracks start at keyways, shoulders and thread roots where stress concentrates. A wet fluorescent examination on a clean, removed shaft is among the most sensitive routine tests available, and a shop can often set one up with a simple bench magnetizing unit and a UV-A lamp.

Field examination is possible when the part cannot be removed. A technician can use a yoke on an installed shaft end, taking care that the contact surface is clean and that nearby bearings and seals will not be harmed by residual magnetism. Where the shaft is important enough to schedule an examination, the owner should also decide in advance whether it will be demagnetized afterward, as stray fields attract steel debris to bearings and can disturb sensors.

Weld repairs on fabricated equipment

Fabrication shops and maintenance departments repair far more often than they build. When a crack is ground out of a frame, a tank attachment or a vessel nozzle, MT confirms that the excavation is clean before welding starts, and again on the finished weld after it has cooled to the temperature the procedure allows. That two-step habit prevents the expensive cycle of welding over a remaining crack tip and finding it again later.

Preheat and heat treatment need coordination with the examination. Dry particles tolerate somewhat warmer surfaces than wet carriers do, and the procedure states the highest temperature allowed. On pressure equipment, repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, and the person authorized to accept the repair makes that decision. Our MT record is one piece of the documentation they review.

Preparing a component for MT

Good preparation shortens the job. Send a list of the items and where they are, the material grade, whether any are coated or galvanized and the surface temperature expected on the day. Let us know whether parts will be removed or examined in place, what power is available and whether the area can be darkened for fluorescent particles. If there is a customer or code procedure, send it, since our technicians work to the version you name. Early answers let us choose dry or wet particles, bring the correct yoke or bench unit and size the crew accurately.

Who performs the work

MT technicians are qualified under a written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician chooses the technique, carries out the examination, interprets indications and writes the record. An ASNT Level III signs off the procedure and the reporting format. The company, not an outside body, issues the certification, as the recommended practice intends.

Where a Richmond owner has its own procedure or a code-specified one, we review and follow it. The Level III consulting service is available when a procedure needs to be written or checked against the code edition.

What the MT report contains

Each report identifies the item and location, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its last calibration, the particle type and carrier, the field direction and number of examinations, the surface condition and the technician and level. Indications are located and measured, described by shape and orientation and documented with photographs or sketches, then accepted or rejected under the named criteria. Parts that needed demagnetization record that it was done.

For repeat inspections of fatigue-sensitive parts, the report can map each face so that the next inspection compares like with like.

Planning an MT job in Richmond

Hot, humid summers make steel surfaces uncomfortable and wet particles dry too fast on sun-heated plate, while cool damp winter days can leave condensation on steel and slow particle mobility. Check the procedure's temperature range and the surface temperature before starting. Thunderstorms and humidity can interrupt outdoor work at plants, terminals and bridge approaches.

Plants usually require badging, safety orientation and permits. Hot-work and electrical rules often apply near flammable processes, and a mains-powered yoke or UV lamp may need approval. Indicate whether power is available, whether wet methods are allowed and whether darkness or a shroud can be arranged for fluorescent work. With I-95 and I-64 meeting in Richmond, travel for a mobilized crew is straightforward, but outage seasons book early.

MT, PT or UT for your Richmond job

Choose MT for fast, sensitive crack detection on carbon and low-alloy steel. Choose PT for non-magnetic metals and awkward shapes. Choose UT in Richmond for wall thickness and the interior of welds. A common sequence is UT to check thickness, MT on the final weld surface. Our MT versus PT comparison explains the choice in more detail, and the national MT page gives an overview.

Training your own MT technicians

Companies that want MT skills in house can begin with MT Level 1 training and move to MT Level 2 training. Atlantis provides the instruction and your company certifies under its own written practice. See the Richmond training page for how classroom theory and practice at your facility combine.

faq.q: What is MT inspection used for in Richmond?
faq.a: It finds surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, such as weld toes on structural steel, crane and hoist parts, shafts and pins, trailer and rail frames, and repair welds on pressure equipment.

faq.q: Which metals cannot be inspected by magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and nickel alloys cannot be magnetized well enough for particles to collect, so dye penetrant inspection is the standard surface method for those metals.

faq.q: Can MT be used on painted steel?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded paint can be examined through if the procedure allows it, though sensitivity drops as the coating gets thicker. Heavy or flaking coatings are removed locally before the examination.

faq.q: Do you use wet or dry particles?
faq.a: It depends on the surface and conditions. Dry powder suits rough or warm field welds, while wet visible or fluorescent particles give better sensitivity on clean, smooth parts. The procedure states the choice.

faq.q: Why is the part magnetized in two directions?
faq.a: A crack is found best when it crosses the magnetic field. Applying the field in two roughly perpendicular directions means cracks of any orientation are examined.

faq.q: Which code sets the MT acceptance criteria in Virginia?
faq.a: The construction code or contract does: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.1 or B31.3, AWS D1.1 or D1.5, or the owner's specification. Virginia's boiler rules require ASME construction for covered equipment.

faq.q: How do I request an MT quote for a Richmond job?
faq.a: Use the quote form to describe the steel, the number of items, the governing code and when access is possible. Our reply, within one business day, either asks follow-up questions or sets out a scoped quotation for a mobilized crew.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Richmond office or lab?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians travel to your plant or fabrication shop, and badging, power supply and safety orientation are agreed with you before they are mobilized.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: When the procedure or a later operation requires it, yes. Residual magnetism can affect welding, machining and bearings, so the procedure states when demagnetizing is needed and the report records it.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Richmond, VA | Dye Check
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection (PT) of welds and parts in stainless, aluminum and steel at Richmond, VA plants, breweries and fabricators. Mobilized to site. Quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Richmond, Virginia
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing (PT, also called dye penetrant inspection) for Richmond and central Virginia owners. PT finds flaws that are open to the surface on welds, castings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel. Typical jobs are process piping and vessel welds at chemical, food and beverage plants and repair welds at fabricators. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send details through the PT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Richmond

The Richmond area has a strong base in process and consumer manufacturing: specialty chemicals, plastics and urethane products, paper and packaging, medical supplies, and an East Coast brewery among its food and beverage plants. Many of those plants run stainless steel and aluminum equipment because product purity and corrosion resistance matter, and those metals cannot be examined with magnetic methods. PT is therefore the routine surface test after a repair weld, a modification or a periodic shutdown.

Fabricators in the region work in carbon steel, stainless and aluminum, building tanks, skids, frames and process equipment. Hospitals and the university medical campus run steam and medical gas systems that include stainless and copper alloy parts, and the Richmond Marine Terminal and associated logistics sites have a mix of equipment and fittings. Penetrant testing covers all these metals with one technique.

What PT finds and what it misses

Penetrant is a thin liquid that is drawn by capillary action into any crack, lap or pore that opens to the surface. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the liquid back out, leaving a colored mark that is far easier to see than the flaw itself. PT is sensitive to fine fatigue cracks, stress corrosion cracks, grinding cracks, weld crater cracks and leak paths through thin walls.

Its limits come from the same mechanism. Only surface-breaking discontinuities are detected: a flaw buried inside the wall, or one whose opening has been smeared shut by grinding or blasting, shows nothing. Porous or very rough surfaces hold penetrant and produce a heavy background that can hide real indications. PT says nothing about wall thickness or internal weld quality, which is the job of UT in Richmond. It also depends on cleanliness: oil, paint, wax and weld residue all keep penetrant out of the crack.

Codes, Virginia rules and acceptance criteria

The method is set out in ASME Section V Article 6, which our Article 6 guide summarizes, and in ASTM E165 for general industry. Acceptance comes from the construction code or contract: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping and AWS D1.1 where it calls for PT.

The Virginia Department of Labor and Industry administers the boiler and pressure vessel safety program under Title 16, Agency 25, Chapter 50 of the Virginia Administrative Code. Covered equipment must be built to ASME rules and registered with the National Board and the state. Inspections come from commissioned insurance company inspectors, contract fee inspectors and owner-user inspectors, and the Department issues the certificate after approving a satisfactory report. PT results can accompany a repair record, but they do not replace the commissioned inspector's role.

The examination sequence

PT proceeds in a strict order. The surface is cleaned with solvent, detergent or mechanical methods and then allowed to dry fully. Penetrant goes on and stays wet for the dwell time in the procedure, long enough to enter tight cracks. Excess is removed, by solvent-dampened wipes on most field jobs, without flushing penetrant out of the flaws. A thin, even coat of developer follows, and the technician examines the surface during and after the development time.

Visible red-dye penetrant with white developer is the usual field choice because it needs no darkened space. Fluorescent penetrant offers higher sensitivity, is generally used in workshops where lighting can be controlled, and requires a UV-A source. After inspection the residue is removed again so it does not interfere with later welding, coating or product contact, which is vital in food, beverage and chemical service.

Cleanliness, chemistry and stainless steel

In stainless and nickel-alloy service, penetrant materials can themselves cause harm if they leave chlorides or sulfur on the metal, which is why specifications often require low-halogen, low-sulfur products with certification for each lot. The procedure names the product family and cleaning agents, and the report lists the lot numbers. Aluminum and titanium can carry similar controls. Product-contact surfaces in a brewery or food plant may also require a documented final cleaning step and compatibility with the plant's own sanitation program.

Ask for these controls up front. A procedure written for carbon steel in a fabrication shop is not automatically suitable for a stainless vessel that will hold a food-grade product, and writing the right procedure first avoids rework.

Temperature and surface preparation

Article 6 provides a standard range of about forty to one hundred twenty-five degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that window the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature in use, normally on a comparator block. In central Virginia, a steel surface in direct summer sun can exceed the upper limit, and an unheated building on a winter morning can fall below the lower one, so temperature is measured and noted rather than assumed.

Surface preparation is equally important. Wire brushing, shot blasting or heavy grinding can smear metal over a crack opening, so where such processes were used, chemical etching or another prescribed step may be needed before penetrant is applied. The procedure states what is acceptable for each material and finish.

Tanks, heat exchangers and process vessels

Process plants are full of vessels with nozzle welds, attachment welds, internal supports and heat exchanger tubesheet joints, and many of them are stainless or clad. PT is the standard surface test on those welds after fabrication, modification or repair, particularly where the weld is accessible from the outside or from an open manway. Because the liquid flows around fillets and into corners, it reveals toe cracks and crater cracks at junctions where other surface methods struggle.

Cladding and overlay deserve a mention. Where stainless or nickel overlay is applied to carbon steel, PT checks the finished surface for cracking and lack of bond at the edges. The report should state the base and overlay materials, since penetrant chemistry and the acceptance criteria can differ. Questions about whether the vessel can be opened and cleaned should be answered before the crew is mobilized.

Machined parts, shafts and fittings

PT is also the quiet workhorse for machined components that will not magnetize or that are too small and complex for other methods: pump impellers and casings, valve bodies and seats, aluminum housings, hydraulic fittings and food-processing parts. Grinding cracks, heat-treatment cracks, fatigue cracks at keyways and leak paths through castings show clearly with the right dwell and a thin developer layer.

Technique choices depend on the part. Smooth machined surfaces call for short dwell times and gentle removal so that tight cracks are not washed out, while rougher castings may need longer cleaning and a post-emulsified or solvent-removable system chosen to control background. The procedure names the system and the acceptance limits, and our technicians record whether each indication is relevant, non-relevant or false.

Information that makes a PT quote accurate

Send a list of the items and where they are, the base metal and any cladding, the finish or coating, the expected surface temperature and whether parts can be removed and cleaned. Tell us the acceptance standard and whether low-halogen materials, lot certification or a final cleaning verification are required. Describe the working environment, from open deck to enclosed manway to workshop bench, and the ventilation available. With that information the crew can bring the correct materials and enough time, avoiding a second trip.

Who performs the work

PT technicians work under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs the sequence, interprets indications and records them, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and report. Employer-based certification means the qualification is a statement about Atlantis's program, not a personal license that moves between employers.

If a Richmond customer has a procedure or a code-specified one, we review and follow it. For owners who need one written, the written practice service and Level III consulting are available.

What the PT report contains

The report names the component, location and drawing or weld number, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with lot numbers, the cleaning method, the surface and part temperature, the dwell and developer times and the technician and level. Indications are described by location, shape and size with photographs and a scale where possible. Relevant indications are separated from non-relevant ones such as machining marks, and each is accepted or rejected under the criteria in your contract.

Planning a PT job in Richmond

Humid summer days slow the evaporation of solvent and can cause sweating on cool steel, while thunderstorms and wind carry dust onto freshly cleaned surfaces. Winter days in the region can drop near or below the procedure's lower limit. For outdoor work, plan windows when surfaces are within the allowed range and protect the area from rain and blowing debris.

PT, MT or UT for your Richmond job

Choose PT for non-magnetic metals and complex shapes. Choose MT in Richmond when the part is carbon or low-alloy steel and speed matters. Choose UT for thickness and internal weld quality. The MT versus PT comparison helps with the decision, and the national PT page gives general detail.

Training your own PT technicians

To build in-house capability, start with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and let trainees practice the sequence on the PT practical simulator. Certification of your staff stays with your company under its own written practice. The Richmond training page explains how this works with hands-on practice at your facility.

faq.q: What is dye penetrant inspection used for in Richmond?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks and porosity on welds, castings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel, which suits chemical, food and beverage plants, fabricators and medical facilities.

faq.q: Can PT detect flaws inside a weld?
faq.a: No. Penetrant only enters discontinuities open to the surface. Internal lack of fusion, slag and wall loss are found with ultrasonic testing, so the two methods are often used together.

faq.q: Why are low-halogen penetrants required on stainless steel?
faq.a: Chlorides and sulfur left on stainless or nickel alloys can cause corrosion or cracking in service. Specifications therefore require certified low-halogen, low-sulfur materials and thorough post-examination cleaning.

faq.q: Can PT be done in cold or hot weather?
faq.a: Only within the procedure's temperature range, which under ASME Article 6 is normally about forty to one hundred twenty-five degrees Fahrenheit unless qualified otherwise. Surface temperature is measured and recorded.

faq.q: Does grinding or blasting affect PT results?
faq.a: Yes. Those processes can smear metal over crack openings and hide them. The procedure states what preparation is acceptable, and etching or other steps may be needed before penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Which code gives PT acceptance limits for Virginia work?
faq.a: The construction code or contract does, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, ASME B31.1 or B31.3, or AWS D1.1. Virginia's boiler rules require ASME construction for covered equipment.

faq.q: How do I request a PT quote in Richmond?
faq.a: Tell us about the metal, the number of items, the code you are working to and the access you can offer. Expect a response from us inside one business day, either with a few follow-up questions or with a scoped quotation covering the technicians who would travel to you.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Richmond?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or shop, and ventilation, solvent rules and orientation are confirmed with you ahead of time.

faq.q: Can PT be used on food-grade equipment?
faq.a: Yes, with the right materials and a documented final cleaning step. The procedure should be written for the product-contact surface so that no residue remains, and your sanitation program may add its own requirements.
